metadata.title: Relationships between teacher education mechanisms and teacher practices, self-efficacy, and job satisfaction in the U.S.: An analysis of TALIS 2018

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study used TALIS 2018’s two-stage complex sampling design (schools sampled with probability proportional to size, then teachers sampled within schools). After filtering the U.S. teacher file to the analytic population (full-time, core-content teachers, single-school teachers, and excluding special education teachers), the authors normalized the sampling weights so they summed to the final analytic sample size. They then used the normalized sampling weight variable (TCHWGT) in the regression estimation and pooled results across five multiply imputed datasets. Replicate weights were not reported; instead, uncertainty from missing data was handled via multiple imputation and regression results were pooled across imputations.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: plausible_values_handling is 'not_applicable' — the study likely does not analyze cognitive achievement PVs (e.g., it may focus on affective/attitudinal outcomes, curriculum data, or non-ILSA micro-data).

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the full U.S. TALIS 2018 teacher dataset filtered to: (1) full-time teachers defined as >90% of full-time hours at the current school (TT3G10A), (2) teachers of core content areas (reading/writing/literature, mathematics, science, social studies; TT3G37), (3) teachers who teach in only one school (TT3G12), and (4) excluded special education teachers (SPED). Final analytic sample comprised 1175 lower-secondary teachers from 164 schools.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel regression (fixed effects; coefficients pooled across 5 multiply imputed datasets, weighted by TCHWGT). No ML metrics (e.g., accuracy/RMSE) reported; Table 2 reports standardized coefficients and SEs.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 (U.S. lower-secondary teachers) the study leveraged teacher cooperation, pre-service content emphases (e.g., student behavior/classroom management and monitoring learning), professional development activities (e.g., peer/self-observation and coaching), and feedback sources (especially principal/management team) to model teacher practices (T3TPRA), finding that teacher cooperation and several pre-service/PD/feedback mechanisms were associated with more favorable teaching practices while ICT-for-teaching emphasis and formal induction at first employer were associated with less favorable practices. This indicates that strengthening collaborative teacher learning and targeted feedback mechanisms may improve classroom practice, though the study is observational and does not support causal claims.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel regression (fixed effects; coefficients pooled across 5 multiply imputed datasets, weighted by TCHWGT). No ML metrics reported; Table 2 reports standardized coefficients and SEs.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 (U.S. lower-secondary teachers) the study leveraged teacher cooperation, pre-service emphasis on teaching cross-curricular skills, and multiple in-service professional development activities (online courses/seminars, education conferences, and peer/self-observation/coaching) to model teacher self-efficacy (T3SELF), finding positive associations for cooperation and these learning mechanisms, while being assigned a mentor was associated with lower self-efficacy. This indicates that designing professional development and collaborative structures that build teachers’ instructional confidence may support self-efficacy, but reverse causality and unmeasured confounding remain plausible in this cross-sectional associational design.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel regression (fixed effects; coefficients pooled across 5 multiply imputed datasets, weighted by TCHWGT). No ML metrics reported; Table 2 reports standardized coefficients and SEs.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 (U.S. lower-secondary teachers) the study leveraged teacher cooperation, pre-service emphasis on multicultural/multilingual settings and monitoring learning, professional development via teacher networks, and feedback from the principal/management team to model teacher job satisfaction (T3JOBSA), finding that cooperation and principal/management feedback were positively associated with satisfaction while multicultural/multilingual preparation was associated with lower satisfaction. This indicates that policies promoting collaborative teacher cooperation and structured administrative feedback may improve retention-relevant satisfaction, while the content emphasis on multicultural/multilingual preparation may require careful implementation context to avoid unintended negative associations.

data.outcome_summary: This associational study used TALIS 2018’s U.S. lower-secondary teacher data, filtered to full-time, core-content, single-school teachers and excluding special education teachers (final analytic sample: 1175 teachers in 164 schools). The authors estimated weighted multilevel regression models (TCHWGT; results pooled across five multiply imputed datasets) for three outcomes: teacher practices (T3TPRA), teacher self-efficacy (T3SELF), and teacher job satisfaction (T3JOBSA). No machine-learning algorithms or predictive performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/RMSE) were reported; instead, Table 2 provides standardized regression coefficients and standard errors. Key predictors included teacher cooperation, specific pre-service content foci (e.g., student behavior/classroom management; monitoring learning), in-service professional development activities (online courses/seminars; conferences; peer/self-observation and coaching; teacher networks), and feedback sources (especially principal/management team). Limitations include observational design (no causal identification), potential measurement error in self-reported practices, and the possibility of reverse causality for mentoring-related findings.
